concept: An agent is a file, and the file's path is its HTTP route — nothing registers it
triggers: how do I serve an agent

lessons.explains: Saving agents/chat.ts serves POST /api/agents/chat. There is no router to touch and no handler to write — what the file exports is the whole endpoint, and .input() is enforced before the agent runs
Every agent declares who may run it; 'public' is a decision rather than the absence of one, and it covers the run, the thread routes, the approval surface and MCP
A state-changing route is CSRF-protected by default: a hand-built fetch without X-Theo-Action gets 403, which reads as a broken agent and is a request that never reached one
The framework refuses a model id whose provider the app never named, so a prefix that works in a plain Agent.create script is rejected before any request leaves the process
Declaring the SDK catalog with .plugins(Provider.builtins()) makes a prefix routable — and a second agent is a second file, needing no more registration than the first

notCovered: the React side: useAgent, the chat UI, and streaming into a component
tools, skills and human-in-the-loop approvals on the agent
server/routes, WebSocket, cron and the rest of the framework's surface
auth: this example's agent is public and has no login

evidence.claims: Starts the real dev server with LLM_MODEL pointed at runtime/fake-provider.ts and asserts over HTTP: an unnamed agent is 404 while agents/chat.ts answers 200 with the provider's text, a body that does not match .input() never reaches the agent, a request without X-Theo-Action is 403, an undeclared provider prefix is refused, and a second agent declaring Provider.builtins() reaches a prefix the first one cannot. It proves the routing, the compilation and the transport. It proves nothing about a model's answer, because the model is a local stub.

Serves the app the way a reader would run it. Without a provider credential the agent route still exists and answers with a provider error rather than 404 — which is itself the proof that the file became a route.
